peak.fp64_source: SM count x FP64 FMA per clock per SM (CUDA C++ Programming Guide, Arithmetic Instructions throughput table, compute capability 7.5: 2) x 2 FLOP per FMA x the device's reported maximum clock (cudaDeviceProp::clockRate)
peak.dram_source: 2 x memory clock (cudaDeviceProp::memoryClockRate) x bus width (cudaDeviceProp::memoryBusWidth) / 8
peak.observed_clock_source: median over N of the median per-repetition clock reading (NVML nvmlDeviceGetClockInfo(NVML_CLOCK_SM), sampled every 0.2 s)

workload.problem: two-body Kepler orbits (mu = 1, float64) from periapsis, a = 1, e uniform in [0, 0.9], random orientation; adaptive RKF7(8) (Fehlberg's tableau, a mixed absolute/relative max-norm error control and a standard step-size controller).
workload.scheme_source: E. Fehlberg, NASA Technical Report R-287 (1968): the RKF7(8) pair
workload.last_step: clipped to land on the final time (a common alternative rejects an overshooting attempt and retries it shortened)

code_lines.rule: non-blank, non-comment lines between the `# >>> code:NAME` and `# <<< code:NAME` markers of the script; every arm but Warp also uses the shared scheme block (the RKF7(8) stages, the right-hand side, the error norm), counted once in shared_scheme_lines

method.warm_up: one run per arm, excluded; it is also the verification run
method.interleaving: the arm order rotates by one every repetition
method.wall: the integration alone, inputs already on the device, to the device synchronised
method.verification: Every arm, every sample: final time reached exactly; position error against the analytic Kepler state (Newton on Kepler's equation to machine precision) below the stated bound n_acc tol (1 + v_p)(1 + 6 pi n_orbits v_p), derived from the controller's per-step budget and the Kepler along-track amplification (see truth_bound; not fitted). Step counts are compared with the reference arm (eagle graph): any difference comes from a floating-point difference flipping one accept/reject decision (contraction into fused multiply-adds, pow and sqrt implementations differ between compilers and libraries); the table reports how many samples differ and by how much.
method.counting_rule: useful FLOPs = FLOPs per attempt x the attempts the samples actually make (accepted + rejected, summed over samples, as counted by the arm itself); 1106 FLOP per attempt: 1099 counted by running the scheme code (rkf78_stages, kepler_rhs, error_ratio) on a counting number (+, -, x, /, abs, max and sqrt one FLOP each; zero coefficients skipped, as every arm skips them) plus 7 in the controller (the clip, the power, the safety factor, the two-sided clamp, the new step, the new time). The same count for every arm: work a masked arm spends on finished samples, and a batched loop spends past a sample's end, is not useful.

memory.method: A separate pass after the timing pass. Each (arm, N) runs in a fresh process: imports, the CUDA context created by one tiny device operation, then the baseline read, before the arm builds or allocates anything; then the arm's kernels built and a warm-up run on a 64-sample batch (every compile happens here; JAX also compiles for shape N), so every library's pool reserved during the warm-up counts in the reading; CuPy's pools and PyTorch's cache trimmed after the warm-up; then the arm built for N (eagle's graph, PyTorch's captured graph) and one full run with upload and download; then the reading again, the allocators still holding their high-water reservation (the same measure for every arm, no sampling needed). Device: the memory NVML accounts to the process on the timed GPU, after minus baseline. Caveats: each allocator's rounding and growth policy count (JAX's allocator grows in regions that can exceed the request; PyTorch rounds blocks up and a captured CUDA graph keeps a private pool; Warp's stream-ordered pool reserves in chunks of tens of MiB, its release threshold set to 0 after the warm-up); the driver accounts in pages of about 2 MiB, so small-N rows read 0 or one page. Host: the peak resident set (VmHWM, reset to the current RSS at the host baseline, taken after the warm-up) minus the baseline RSS. Minimum: the planes the workload needs, N x (8 float64 planes (state, time, step) x 8 bytes + 2 counters x 4 bytes) = N x 72 bytes.

compile_time.method: Its own pass, never part of any wall. Each measurement is a fresh process: imports and the GPU context run untimed, then the timer spans the first call to a ready kernel (trace + code generation + compile + load, or the cache lookup). Cold: every cache empty (HAWK_CACHE_DIR, CUPY_CACHE_DIR, CUDA_CACHE_PATH, WARP_CACHE_PATH and JAX's persistent compilation cache, each a fresh directory); warm: a new process on the caches the first cold run populated. eagle GPU: eagle.deploy of the hawk attempt kernel and of its active-set variant (host and device builds each), and one eagle graph of each built and run on 64 samples (eagle.simulate deploys the first again, a cache hit). eagle CPU: the same eagle.deploy of the attempt kernel (host and device builds) and one host run. CuPy: one masked attempt on 64 samples (every elementwise kernel compiled on first use). JAX: lower + compile from abstract shapes at N. Warp: the kernel module (code generation, compile, load) and one launch. Medians of 3 cold and 3 warm processes.

rows.what: eagle.deploy of the attempt kernel and its active-set variant
eagle.deploy of the attempt kernel, host run

fit.intro: Each tool here solves the same 13-stage adaptive problem to the same tolerance and agrees with the analytic orbit; they differ in how the per-sample control flow is written and run. Numbers below are at N = 1,000,000; the fastest arm there is eagle.simulate (eagle picks the launch mode) (4.26 s).

arms.eagle_graph: the attempt is per-sample scalar code (22 lines with its launch; the kernel finishes its own samples), one kernel per attempt looped on the device: 7.39 s.
arms.eagle_graph_compact: the same kernel launched over the live samples only: 4.41 s; the plain graph takes 1.68× as long.
arms.eagle_graph_reorder: adds the occasional reorder of the planes: 4.3 s; the compacted graph takes 1.03× as long.
arms.eagle_graph_persist: the plain (not active-set) attempt kernel, forced through hawk's persist entry: one launch, no graph, no map, no policy kernel -- a grid of SMs blocks of 256 lanes steals the next unfinished sample off a counter when their own finishes: 4.26 s; the eagle graph takes 1.73× as long.
arms.eagle_simulate: the same kernel through eagle.simulate, its state and parameters by name (21 lines with the kernel): 4.26 s; the eagle graph takes 1.73× as long.
arms.cupy_masked: array code in the NumPy style (25 lines), the control flow as masks over the batch: 89.9 s.
arms.torch_masked: the same array formulation in PyTorch (27 lines), running where a PyTorch model already runs: 95.1 s.
arms.torch_graphed: records 16 attempts as a CUDA graph and replays them, removing per-kernel launch cost: 95.4 s; eager PyTorch takes 0.998× as long.
arms.jax_vmap: writes the per-sample loop directly (25 lines) and compiles the whole batch into one executable: 13.1 s.
arms.warp_kernel: an explicit per-thread loop in a Python-embedded kernel language (74 lines, its own stages): 7.88 s.
arms.eagle_cpu: the same hawk kernel on the host's cores, no GPU needed: 36.1 s.
